This page goes with **Chapter 29, Voice Leading Chromatic Harmonies** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/VoiceLeadingChromaticHarmonies.html). Read each section there first. It builds on [Chapter 17, Secondary Dominants](secondary-dominants.qmd), [18, Secondary Diminished Chords](secondary-diminished.qmd),
[19, Mode Mixture](mode-mixture.qmd), [20, The Neapolitan Chord](neapolitan.qmd) and [Voice Leading Seventh Chords](voice-leading-sevenths.qmd).

**How the page works.** Each example is drawn on a grand staff, plays when you press **Play**, and is **marked by the same checker** that marks your exercises: a green *Right*
passes it, a red *Wrong* shows what the checker says. In the exercises the given notes are greyed; type the others (`E4`, `F#4`, `Bb3`; **Up** and **Down** move a step in the key,
**Shift** a half step) and press **Check**.


## 29.1 Secondary chords

Voice lead a secondary chord as you would a seventh chord: **resolve the 7th down by step**, and alternate complete and incomplete voicings in a row of root position sevenths. The chord's
third (the temporary leading tone, a raised note) rises by a half step to the root of the chord it points to, and so **cancels** the chromatic note. The leading-tone rules apply to the temporary leading tone too.
One exception from the book: when V<sup>7</sup>/V or vii&deg;/V goes to V and the melody needs the seventh above the third, write parallel (unequal) fifths rather than double the leading tone.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["V7/V","A4 F#4 C4 D3"],["V","G4 G4 B3 G3"]]'>V7/V to V: F# (the leading tone of V) rises to G, the seventh C falls to B.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="leaptone" data-rows='[["V7/V","A4 F#4 C4 D3"],["V","G4 D4 B3 G3"]]'>The raised F# (the leading tone of V) in the alto falls to D instead of rising to G.</div>


## 29.2 Borrowed chords

Borrowed (mode mixture) chords are voiced like their diatonic versions: iv like IV, for instance. Whenever scale degree 6 is a member of a borrowed chord, **resolve it down by step**.
The same goes for the cadential vii&deg;7 (borrowed): rise the third of the chord up by step and move the other voices in contrary motion, as in the deceptive cadence in minor.
There are no special rules for other borrowed chords: move smoothly and avoid objectionable parallels.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["iv","F4 C4 Ab3 F3"],["V","D4 B3 G3 G3"]]'>iv in C major (borrowed): its A&#9837; (6&#9837;) falls to G.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="borrowed6" data-rows='[["iv","F4 C4 Ab3 F3"],["I","E4 C4 C4 C3"]]'>The A&#9837; leaps up to C instead of falling.</div>


## 29.3 The Neapolitan chord

Two rules for N<sup>6</sup> in four parts: **double the bass** (the third of the chord) and **resolve 2&#9837;** (the root of N, a half step above 1) **down** to the nearest note of the next chord.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["N6","Ab4 F4 Db4 F3"],["V","G4 D4 B3 G3"]]'>N6 doubles its bass F; the D&#9837; falls to B (the nearest note of V).</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="neapolitan" data-rows='[["N6","Db5 Ab4 Db4 F3"]]'>N6 should double its bass F, not the root D&#9837;.</div>


## 29.4 Augmented sixth chords

The salient accidental in every augmented sixth chord is &#9839;4, which almost always resolves **up to 5**, including when the chord goes to the cadential I<sup>6</sup><sub>4</sub>. In the
enharmonic German chord, 2 and 4 rise to members of a major chord. The exception: when an augmented sixth chord goes to V<sup>7</sup>, &#9839;4 goes to 4&#9838;, which is the seventh of V<sup>7</sup>. Otherwise move all voices smoothly, avoid parallels and double properly.
*The checker does not read augmented sixth chord symbols: they are left for you and your teacher.*

## 29.5 Exercises

**One. V7/V to V to I.** The soprano holds C (the seventh of V7/V) and then falls to B.

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="C" data-hint="V7/V is D F# A C. F# rises to G, the seventh C falls to B." data-rows='[{"rn":"I","S":"C5","B":"C3"},{"rn":"V7/V","S":"C5","B":"D3"},{"rn":"V","S":"B4","B":"G3"},{"rn":"I","S":"C5","B":"C3"}]'></div>

**Two. A borrowed iv.**

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="C" data-hint="iv is F Ab C: write Ab with the flat (`Ab3`); it falls to G in V." data-rows='[{"rn":"I","S":"G4","B":"C3"},{"rn":"iv","S":"F4","B":"F3"},{"rn":"V","S":"D4","B":"G3"},{"rn":"I","S":"E4","B":"C3"}]'></div>

**Three. N6 to V to I.**

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="C" data-hint="N6 is Db F Ab: write the flats (`Db4`, `Ab3`). Double the bass F; the Db falls to the nearest note of V." data-rows='[{"rn":"I","S":"G4","B":"C3"},{"rn":"N6","S":"F4","B":"F3"},{"rn":"V","S":"D4","B":"G3"},{"rn":"I","S":"E4","B":"C3"}]'></div>


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the checker does and does not check
- Secondary chords: the seventh and the (temporary) leading tone are checked as in chapter 27. Borrowed chords: scale degree 6 resolves down; the Neapolitan doubles its bass and its root falls. Everything from chapters 26 to 28 applies.
- **Not checked:** the V7/V to V unequal-fifths exception (the checker flags the doubled leading tone as written, and warns about unequal fifths), augmented sixth chords, and borrowed chords other than iv / bVI.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
